title: AI-led resilience is colliding with inflation, public-debt, non-bank, and digital-money risks that test financial stability and trust
source_unit: Bank for International Settlements, Annual Economic Report 2026
geography: Global monetary, financial, fiscal, AI-investment, supply-shock, non-bank, and digital-money systems

denominator.unit: global economy, trade, financial conditions, and AI-investment frame

resilience.value: the global economy absorbed tariff and conflict shocks with support from AI-related investment and favourable financial conditions

risk_channels.value: persistent inflation risks, sustainability of AI investment, financial vulnerabilities, and weakening fiscal positions are mounting pressure points

policy_priority.value: price stability, fiscal sustainability, financial stability, and structural reform are mutually reinforcing priorities

observations.method: BIS global macroeconomic, monetary, financial-market, fiscal, and structural analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The report is a policy assessment, not a deterministic forecast; resilience and risk can differ across economies, sectors, borrowers, and households.
observations.subgroup: Households exposed to inflation and borrowing costs, workers, firms investing in AI, governments, central banks, and financial institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI investment may raise productivity and broaden growth capacity, while credible policy can contain inflation and financial risk without suppressing productive innovation.

observations.period: 2026; public debt and the fiscal-financial stability nexus

denominator.unit: public debt, sovereign debt markets, non-bank financial intermediation, and monetary-policy transmission frame

debt_pressure.value: public debt is near record highs in many economies

non_bank_role.value: non-banks play a growing role in sovereign debt markets

stress_transmission.value: the fiscal-financial stability nexus can amplify and accelerate market stress and complicate monetary-policy transmission

observations.method: BIS analysis of public debt, sovereign markets, non-bank finance, and central-bank policy transmission.
observations.uncertainty: The global framing does not identify which countries or households will bear future adjustment costs, nor does it predict a specific market event.
observations.subgroup: Borrowers, savers, pension funds, governments, taxpayers, non-bank financial institutions, banks, and households dependent on public services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Non-bank finance can diversify funding and absorb risk when transparency, liquidity management, capital, and macroprudential safeguards are adequate.

observations.period: 2026; supply shocks, energy costs, and household room

denominator.unit: global supply-shock, energy-input, inflation, and household purchasing-power frame

shock_context.value: major supply shocks and geopolitical conflict remain in motion

input_cost_channel.value: disruption around critical energy and shipping routes can lift input costs and weigh on growth

household_translation.value: price stability affects real purchasing power, borrowing conditions, employment, and the room households have for discretionary consumption

observations.method: BIS integration of macroeconomic, financial, geopolitical, and supply-shock analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Aggregate inflation and input-cost channels do not estimate a household's actual basket, debt service, wage adjustment, or consumption response.
observations.subgroup: Low-income households, energy-intensive firms, importers, workers, borrowers, consumers, and economies exposed to maritime or commodity disruption.
observations.counterinterpretation: Supply chains can reroute, inventories and substitution can buffer costs, and policy responses can redistribute or reduce short-run exposure.

observations.period: 2026; digital innovation, stablecoins, and trust in money

denominator.unit: digital-money, programmable-platform, payment, and monetary-trust frame

innovation_channel.value: digital innovation is transforming finance and creating new programmable-platform and money-like instruments

trust_question.value: the policy challenge is preserving trust in money while financial architecture changes

consumer_surface.value: new payment and financial instruments can alter access, convenience, privacy, fraud exposure, and the boundary between public and private money

observations.method: BIS analysis of monetary architecture, digital innovation, stablecoins, programmable platforms, and trust in money.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish individual adoption, consumer welfare, or causal effects of any particular digital-money design; implementation and regulation remain open.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, payment users, banks, non-banks, technology firms, central banks, public institutions, and people with limited financial or digital access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Well-designed digital systems can improve competition, settlement, inclusion, and user control when public safeguards and interoperability are credible.

related_sources.claim: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 PDF provides the full chapter and key-takeaway evidence for AI investment, debt, financial stability, supply shocks, and digital money.
The prior BIS Annual Economic Report provides comparative context for the longer-run monetary and financial-policy discussion.

boundary: This record adds a global central-bank and financial-stability route across AI investment, inflation, public debt, non-bank finance, supply shocks, digital money, and trust. It uses aggregate policy analysis and system-level evidence, not household financial diaries, individual portfolio behavior, causal AI employment estimates, or a forecast of a particular crisis.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 materials were reviewed for AI-related resilience, inflation and financial vulnerabilities, public debt and non-bank transmission, supply shocks, and digital-money trust.
